blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Every DataFrame you have built so far in this course could be shuffled row by row and lose nothing. Sort a table of customers by name instead of by signup date, and every row still means exactly what it meant before. Time series data does not work that way. A stock price, a sensor reading, a server's CPU usage logged every minute, all of it depends on its neighbors. Yesterday's closing price is not just another data point sitting somewhere in the table, it is direct context for understanding today's price. Move it, drop it, or process it out of order, and you have quietly broken the meaning of the data. That is exactly why time series gets its own dedicated module in this course, not just a few extra methods bolted onto the DataFrame skills you already have.

blocks.caption: In a time series, position in time is the context. In a normal table, row order rarely matters at all.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442560612-37462102.png

Order and continuity are the two things that change everything. A gap in a table of customers is just a missing customer. A gap in a time series, a day where no reading was recorded, can quietly break every rolling average, every trend calculation, and every model built on top of it later in this module. pandas has an entire dtype and an entire index type built specifically to respect this, and that is what this lesson is about.

items: Order matters: a time series has a natural before and after that a normal table does not.
Continuity matters: gaps and irregular spacing change what calculations like rolling averages actually mean.
Position carries meaning: a row's neighbors are part of its context, not just other unrelated rows in the same table.

blocks.text: You already met pd.to_datetime() and the dt accessor earlier in this course, when converting a messy text column into a real date and when pulling features like day of week out of it. Both of those lessons deliberately stopped at the surface level. This lesson goes underneath: what a datetime64 value actually is, how to make a datetime column the backbone of your DataFrame instead of just another column, and how to handle the timezone traps that catch almost everyone at least once.
2. The datetime64 Dtype Under the Hood

Recall from the NumPy Fundamentals module that every NumPy array has a dtype, a fixed, uniform type that describes how each element is stored in memory, things like int64 or float64. pandas' datetime64 is really just another one of those fixed width NumPy dtypes, and understanding what it stores underneath changes how you think about every date in your DataFrame.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

ts = pd.Timestamp("2024-01-15")
print(ts.value)
# 1705276800000000000

blocks.text: That giant number is not a coincidence or a formatting quirk. Under the hood, a datetime64 value is a single 64 bit integer counting nanoseconds since a fixed reference point: midnight, January 1st 1970, also known as the Unix epoch. January 15th 2024 is simply the moment 1,705,276,800,000,000,000 nanoseconds after that reference point. Every date and time your DataFrame stores, no matter how it looks when you print it, is really just one integer relative to that same starting line.

blocks.alt: The datetime64 Dtype Under the Hood
blocks.caption: Every datetime64 value is really this single integer wearing a human readable disguise.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442560612-888098197.png

blocks.title: Why January 1970 specifically
blocks.content: There is no deep reason beyond convention. Unix systems picked that moment as their reference point decades ago, and nearly every modern data tool, pandas included, inherited it. You never need to think about the epoch directly, just know it is there underneath every timestamp you work with.

blocks.text: 2.1 Why This Makes Datetime Arithmetic So Fast

This is exactly why datetime arithmetic in pandas is so fast. Subtracting one Timestamp from another does not involve parsing calendars, counting days in each month, or worrying about leap years at the moment of calculation. It reduces to plain integer subtraction on two 64 bit numbers, the same kind of vectorized integer math NumPy already does extremely well.

code.content:
a = pd.Timestamp("2024-02-01")
b = pd.Timestamp("2024-01-15")
diff = a - b
print(diff)
# 17 days

print((a.value - b.value) / 1e9 / 86400)
# 17.0, the same answer computed from raw integers

blocks.alt: Why This Makes Datetime Arithmetic So Fast
blocks.caption: Timestamp subtraction is integer subtraction wearing a Timedelta costume.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442560613-119797344.png

This is also why a whole column of datetime64 values behaves like any other NumPy array under the hood, an array of int64 numbers that pandas knows how to format as readable dates. Comparing, sorting, and subtracting an entire column of dates is just as vectorized and just as fast as any other NumPy operation you learned in the earlier module.

blocks.title: The nanosecond range limit
blocks.content: Because it is a 64 bit integer counting nanoseconds, datetime64[ns] can only represent dates from roughly the year 1677 to the year 2262. Anything outside that range overflows the integer and raises an error. This almost never matters for real world data, but it is a direct, visible consequence of what a datetime64 value actually is under the hood.

blocks.text: 3. Setting a Datetime Column as the Index

So far in this course, a DataFrame's index has mostly been an afterthought, the default 0, 1, 2 row numbers pandas assigns automatically. For time series work, the index becomes the single most important structural decision you make. Once a column holds proper datetime64 values, set_index() promotes that column into the DataFrame's index, turning it from just another column into the thing every row is organized by.

code.content:
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
df = df.set_index("date")
print(df.index)
# DatetimeIndex(['2024-01-01', '2024-01-02', ...], dtype='datetime64[ns]', name='date', freq=None)

blocks.alt: Setting a Datetime Column as the Index
blocks.caption: set_index turns a datetime column into the structural backbone of the DataFrame.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442560613-661639134.png
Notice the type of that index in the output: DatetimeIndex, not the plain RangeIndex a fresh DataFrame gets by default. That specific index type is what unlocks everything else in this lesson.
3.1 Why the Index, Not Just a Column

You could, in principle, leave the date as an ordinary column and never touch the index at all. Nothing stops you. But a plain integer index treats row 47 as just row 47, it has no idea that row 47 happens to represent March 3rd. A DatetimeIndex, by contrast, knows it is holding dates, and pandas gives it date aware powers that a regular column, and a regular index, simply do not have. The next section is exactly that payoff.
4. Date Based Slicing With a DatetimeIndex

This is the single biggest reason to bother setting a datetime column as the index at all. Once your index is a proper DatetimeIndex, you can slice straight into it using nothing but a date string, and pandas understands exactly what you mean.

That one line pulls out every row whose index falls anywhere in January 2024, an entire month selected with a plain string. No boolean mask, no comparing year and month columns by hand, no writing out a condition on df.index.year and df.index.month together. pandas parses "2024-01" as a partial date, figures out the full range it covers, and slices directly.

blocks.alt: Date Based Slicing With a DatetimeIndex
blocks.caption: One partial date string, an entire month of rows, no boolean mask required.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442561051-674110545.png

blocks.title: Keep it sorted
blocks.content: Date based slicing works best, and is fastest, when the DatetimeIndex is already sorted in order. Most real data arrives sorted already, but if you are ever unsure, df.sort_index() fixes it in one call before you start slicing.

blocks.text: 4.1 Slicing a Range of Dates
The same trick extends to a range. Give pandas a start date and an end date, separated by a colon just like a normal Python slice, and it returns every row whose index falls between them.

blocks.caption: A date range slice pulls out exactly the window you name, both ends included.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442561053-548098390.png

blocks.title: Both ends are included
blocks.content: Unlike a normal Python list slice, where the end index is excluded, a DatetimeIndex range slice like this one includes both endpoints. df["2024-01-15":"2024-02-01"] includes February 1st itself, not just up to the day before it.

{"headers":["Index type","Slice by month string","Slice by date range"],"rows":[["Plain RangeIndex (0, 1, 2, ...)","Not supported","Not supported"],["DatetimeIndex","Supported, e.g. df[\"2024-01\"]","Supported, e.g. df[\"2024-01-15\":\"2024-02-01\"]"]]}

blocks.text: That difference is the entire practical argument for setting a datetime column as the index in the first place. A regular column supports none of this. An index does.
5. Timezone Awareness

Every Timestamp you have used so far in this lesson has been naive: a date and a time with no information about which timezone that time is actually in. 9:30 AM on its own does not say 9:30 AM where. Naive timestamps work fine right up until you need to compare data collected in different timezones, or hand data off to a system that expects timezone aware values, at which point the missing information becomes a real problem.

blocks.caption: A naive timestamp knows the clock time but has no idea which timezone that clock belongs to.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442561053-275625157.png
5.1 tz_localize: Attaching a Timezone to Naive Data

tz_localize() takes a naive datetime and attaches a timezone label to it, without changing the underlying clock time at all. You are telling pandas what timezone this naive data was always in, not converting it to a different one.

blocks.alt: tz_localize: Attaching a Timezone to Naive Data
blocks.caption: tz_localize labels naive data with a timezone, it does not shift the clock time.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442561054-198810097.png
5.2 tz_convert: Switching an Already Aware Timestamp to a Different Timezone

tz_convert() is the other half of the pair, and it only works on data that is already timezone aware. Where tz_localize attaches a label without moving the clock, tz_convert actually shifts the wall clock time so it displays correctly in a new timezone, while still pointing at the exact same instant.

blocks.alt: tz_convert: Switching an Already Aware Timestamp to a Different Timezone
blocks.caption: tz_convert moves the same instant onto a different timezone's clock.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442561054-357058785.png

blocks.content: {"headers":["Method","Starting point","What it does"],"rows":[["tz_localize","Naive, no timezone attached","Attaches a timezone label, clock time stays the same"],["tz_convert","Aware, already has a timezone","Shifts the clock time to a different timezone, same instant"]]}

blocks.text: 5.3 The Naive Versus Aware Mixing Bug

Here is the genuinely common real world bug: mixing a naive datetime with a timezone aware one in the same operation. It happens more often than you would expect, one column gets localized and another does not, or you join two DataFrames built at different points in a pipeline, one timezone aware and one not. pandas refuses to guess which timezone the naive side belongs to, and raises an error instead.

code.content:
naive = pd.Timestamp("2024-01-15 09:30:00")
aware = pd.Timestamp("2024-01-15 09:30:00", tz="UTC")

naive < aware
# TypeError: Cannot compare tz-naive and tz-aware timestamps

blocks.alt: The Naive Versus Aware Mixing Bug
blocks.caption: pandas will not guess a timezone for you, mixing naive and aware data fails loudly instead of silently.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442561054-313231018.png

blocks.title: How to actually fix it
blocks.content: There is no shortcut around this, you have to make both sides agree. Either localize the naive side with tz_localize so it becomes aware, or strip the timezone off the aware side, whichever matches what the rest of your pipeline expects. The fix is simple, the hard part is noticing the mismatch exists before pandas throws the error at you.

blocks.text: 6. DatetimeIndex Attributes

You already know the dt accessor from earlier in this course, the way df["date"].dt.year pulls the year out of an ordinary datetime64 column. Once that same information lives in the index instead of a column, you do not need the dt accessor at all. A DatetimeIndex exposes the exact same set of date components directly as attributes.

blocks.caption: The DatetimeIndex mirrors the dt accessor, just without needing dt at all.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442561055-245849277.png

blocks.content: {"headers":["Index attribute","Returns"],"rows":[["index.year","The year of every timestamp in the index"],["index.month","The month, 1 through 12, of every timestamp"],["index.day","The day of the month of every timestamp"],["index.dayofweek","0 through 6 for Monday through Sunday"],["index.quarter","Which of the four business quarters each timestamp falls in"]]}

blocks.text: You can combine these attributes with boolean filtering exactly the way you would with the dt accessor. For example, readings[readings.index.dayofweek >= 5] pulls out every weekend row directly from the index, no separate column required.

Everything you learned about extracting date components with dt still applies conceptually, it has just moved from a column level operation to an index level attribute. The two are close enough that switching between them is mostly a matter of remembering whether your dates currently live in a column or in the index.
7. Worked Example: Daily Readings Sliced to One Month
Put the whole lesson together on a small, realistic dataset: 90 days of daily temperature readings from a single sensor, starting January 1st 2024.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

data = {
    "date": pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=90, freq="D"),
    "temperature": [round(5 + i * 0.15, 1) for i in range(90)],
}
readings = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(readings.head())

blocks.text: Right now, date is just an ordinary column, and readings has the default integer index. The first step is converting date to datetime64, if it were not already, and promoting it into the index.

code.content:
readings["date"] = pd.to_datetime(readings["date"])
readings = readings.set_index("date")
print(readings.index)
# DatetimeIndex(['2024-01-01', '2024-01-02', ..., '2024-03-30'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', name='date', freq='D')

blocks.text: With a proper DatetimeIndex in place, pulling out exactly one month of readings, January, is a single line.

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Daily Readings Sliced to One Month
blocks.caption: Same pattern as every example in this lesson: set the index, then slice by date.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442561055-978481004.png

31 rows out of the original 90, every single one of them from January, pulled out without writing a single boolean condition. That is the entire payoff of treating your datetime column as the index instead of just another column sitting in the DataFrame.
8. Recap

items: Time series data gets its own module because a row's meaning is tied to its position in time relative to its neighbors, not just to the values inside that row.
datetime64 is really a 64 bit integer counting nanoseconds since January 1st 1970, which is exactly why datetime arithmetic reduces to fast integer math.
set_index() promotes a datetime64 column into a DatetimeIndex, turning dates from just another column into the DataFrame's organizing structure.
A DatetimeIndex unlocks direct date based slicing: an entire month with a string like 2024-01, or a range between two dates, neither of which works on a plain integer index.
A naive timestamp has no timezone attached, tz_localize attaches one to naive data, and tz_convert shifts already aware data onto a different timezone's clock.
Mixing naive and timezone aware datetimes in the same comparison raises a TypeError, pandas will not silently guess which timezone the naive side belongs to.
A DatetimeIndex exposes year, month, day, dayofweek and more directly as attributes, the same information the dt accessor gives you at the column level.

blocks.text: This lesson focused on the foundation: what a datetime64 value actually is, and how to use a DatetimeIndex to slice and organize your data by date. The rest of this module builds directly on top of it. Timestamp goes deeper into the single datetime object itself, Date Range covers generating sequences of dates from scratch, and Resampling and Rolling Window, coming up soon, are where a properly set DatetimeIndex really starts to pay off.
